blogs.title: Can an e‑Mail Sap Against Statutory Prerequisites? The Fifth Circuit’s Plunge into Digital Cancellation
blogs.description: This post unpacks the Fifth Circuit’s treatment of the “receipt” and “private carrier” language in La. Rev. Stat. §9:3550(G)(3).  It examines whether a computer‑generated e‑Mail can satisfy a statutory requirement originally drafted in an era of paper correspondence, and how the court’s expansive reading of “private carrier” preserves the statute’s intent while avoiding the pitfalls of statutory literalism.  The analysis will explore precedent such as Huntley v. Bayer and Benitez v. Elsayed, and will consider the broader implications for modern insurance‑financing practices where automation increasingly replaces traditional hand‑shaken delivery.  Lawyers and insurer risk managers will find a detailed breakdown of the statutory machinery and a roadmap for compliant digital cancellation workflows.

blogs.title: Signature‑Dead Statutes? The Fifth Circuit’s Flat‑Take on ‘Certifying’ in Insurance‑Financing Law
blogs.description: This post focuses on the heart of Williams v. GoAuto: does §9:3550(G)(3)(a) require a physical signature on the notice of cancellation, or can certification be achieved by a corporate statement alone?  By comparing the Fifth Circuit’s analysis to prior Louisiana opinions—Delatte, Eaglin, Hodges, Benitez, and others—we explore the evolution of the “certifying” concept.  The post will also assess the potential impact of a signature requirement on the administrative burden of finance companies and the legal certainty of insurers, offering a forward‑looking critique of how Louisiana’s legislature might clarify the statute in future codifications.

blogs.title: From Shared Filing Cabinets to Web Services: How Louisiana’s Cancellation Statute Lagged Behind Tech
blogs.description: This post examines the structural and procedural changes GoAuto and APAC have made—from shared filing cabinets to automated web‑service callbacks—and how the court navigated the gap between statutory language and contemporary business practices.  We will evaluate the Fifth Circuit’s reasoning that a modern web‑service call, essentially a “receipt” of a cancellation notice, satisfies the statute, and discuss whether this interpretation sets a durable precedent or merely adapts the rule to an emergent era.  The piece will also consider potential litigation pitfalls for insurers who may still rely on outdated cancellation workflows.

blogs.title: Certifying vs. Re‑certifying: Why the Fifth Circuit Wouldn’t Trek Alabama‑style Certifiability to the Louisiana Supreme Court
blogs.description: Centered on the Fifth Circuit’s refusal to certify the statutory questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, this post analyses the court’s jurisprudential calculus and the broader implications for the court’s certification discipline.  It contrasts the Fifth Circuit’s view with the 5th Circuit’s own precedent in Jefferson v. Lead Indus. and other relevant cases to understand when the court deems a certification “compelling.”  Our discussion will outline how the refusal to seek super‑state guidance affects Louisiana’s insurance law development and may influence how insurers structure their policies and financing agreements to mitigate uncertainty.
